analysis.one_liner: Allows Americans to legally buy lower-priced prescription drugs from certified Canadian pharmacies.
analysis.headline: The bill, with 22 cosponsors, was referred to the Senate health committee in February 2017 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the FDA, within 180 days, to write rules letting wholesalers, pharmacies, and individuals import prescription drugs from Canada. Canadian sellers would have to be licensed and certified by the FDA, and individuals could buy up to a 90-day supply with a valid prescription. After two years, the FDA could expand importation to other countries with comparable drug-approval standards.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who pay US prices for prescription drugs, especially people on fixed incomes paying out of pocket, because many of the same drugs sell for less in Canada. Wholesalers and pharmacies could import at the lower price and pass savings on. Licensed Canadian pharmacies would gain a new, legal US customer base.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the FDA to issue regulations within 180 days permitting wholesalers, pharmacies, and individuals to import qualifying prescription drugs from Canada.
Lets individuals import up to a 90-day supply for personal use from a certified, licensed foreign pharmacy, with a valid US prescription.
After two years, authorizes the FDA to permit importation from other countries that are OECD members with drug-approval standards comparable to the United States.
Makes it unlawful for manufacturers to charge certified foreign sellers higher prices than local buyers, or to restrict, delay, or refuse supply to them to block importation.
Adds penalties of up to 10 years in prison or a $250,000 fine for websites selling adulterated or counterfeit drugs or dispensing without a valid prescription.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who currently charge much higher prices in the US than in Canada and other wealthy countries, would lose that price gap. The FDA's certification and testing program would be funded by fees on the foreign sellers rather than taxpayers.

drawbacks.text: Importation creates safety and supply-chain risks; the bill addresses them with seller certification, recall notification, testing laboratories, and suspension authority, but critics argue the FDA would still struggle to police a cross-border supply chain.

Canada's drug supply is sized for its own population, and Canadian officials and pharmacists have long objected to large-scale export of their medicines, raising the possibility of shortages in Canada and supply limits that shrink the savings available.
The bill prohibits manufacturers from discriminating against importers, but enforcement against global manufacturers with many ways to structure pricing and supply could be difficult in practice.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential savings are large for people who pay US drug prices, and the bill builds in substantial safety machinery: certified sellers, FDA testing, recall requirements, and criminal penalties for counterfeit online pharmacies. The honest objections are that safety oversight of a foreign supply chain is genuinely hard, Canada may not be able or willing to supply a much larger market, and manufacturers would fight importation through pricing and supply tactics even though the bill bans them. On balance it is a real, if imperfect, attempt to lower drug prices.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee in February 2017, and the committee never took it up, so it died when that Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Senator Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on February 28, 2017, joined by 22 cosponsors (21 Democrats and 1 independent).
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action was recorded; the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote in the 115th Congress.
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, and the bill expired.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers kept the US market closed to lower-priced imports and their existing pricing intact. Americans paying US drug prices, and the senators who backed the bill, got nothing.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on February 28, 2017 and took no action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Lamar Alexander
against.what_they_did: As committee chairman, never scheduled a markup or hearing on the bill.

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Brand-name drug manufacturers and their lobbying arm
against.what_they_did: Opposed drug importation legislation, arguing it would undermine safety and undercut patent-protected pricing; the industry has long lobbied against importation bills.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat or independent; no Republicans backed the bill, and the Republican-controlled Senate committee and chamber took no action on it.

industries.note: These companies charge far higher prices in the US than the same drugs sell for in Canada; importation would expose US customers to those lower prices and cut their revenue. The bill also bans their tactics for cutting off supply to importers.
Certified Canadian sellers would gain a large new legal market of American customers. Their gain depends on delivering lower prices to US buyers, so their interest runs with the public's here.
The bill creates significant new certification, testing, and enforcement work for the FDA, funded by fees on foreign sellers rather than taxpayers.
